speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
When the house rose last
night I was trying to establish that, under the law and regulations as they stand at present, the minister had the authority if he saw fit to cancel a license which had been issued. There is no doubt at all that this power exists and that on certain occasions when the reasons justify his doing so the minister may exercise it. Some hon, gentlemen have contended that there is not very much difference between the cancellation of a license, as the word has been used, and the non-renewal of it. I submit there is a great difference. Cancellation means the confiscation of something which exists; the cancellation of a license may take place in the course of the year for which the license has been issued. The renewal of a license, on the other hand, implies the reviving of something which has ceased to exist. All licenses expire on March 31 and they must be renewed; and they are renewed if the minister and the government are satisfied that they should be. It is quite proper that this power should rest with the minister because it can be invoked effectively and advantageously to reduce the number of broadcasting stations in the country. As we all know, the United States are having considerable difficulty in reducing the number of their broadcasting stations. They have too many stations there, it is admitted, and an effort is being made to reduce the number. The situation is somewhat similar in Canada. Personally I am inclined to think that we have too many broadcasting stations here. The proper way to reduce the number of broadcasting stations would be to make use of the power which is given to the minister to not renew licenses when they expire.
Was that the reason this license was not renewed?

No. That may be considered, in part because it may be advantageous to the department and to- the public at large
IMr. Lapointe.]
to have the opportunity of accommodating other firms or companies which may ask for licenses to broadcast. In fact, up to the present time we have refused almost one hundred applications for broadcasting licenses because we felt that the circumstances did not justify the department in granting those requests. The number of wave lengths at our disposal is not very great, and it is always to the advantage of the general public for us to have a certain number of wave lengths free, which we can grant to important companies or organizations upon application being made by them.
One might say that in not renewing the licenses we may be damaging persons or associations or companies who enjoyed these licenses the previous year. When these people make application for licenses they know that these licenses are good for only one year; they enter into those contracts knowing all the facts of the case and knowing that the licenses granted to them state very clearly that they are issued for only one year. It may be that this period is too short and that we should extend the time in order to give the company o-r association an opportunity to secure some return on tihe expenditure made in putting the station in operation.

Just on that point, does the minister seriously suggest that any company is going to spend $150,000, as I understand this Toronto company did, on the understanding that the license may be cancelled in one year? Is it not the practice in connection with these licenses, as in other matters, to extend the licenses from year to year unless there is good reason for cancelling them? We have not heard those reasons as yet.

Certainly not. People who spend large amounts of money in establishing broadcasting stations certainly expect that their license will be continued for more than one year, but when they make their application and when the license is granted it is apparent, to them from the documents and from the law and regulations that their license can be taken away from them. Supposing the company to which my hon. friend has referred, a big company in Toronto, or elsewhere, spent $150,000 or $200,000 to establish a broadcasting station; let us imagine that there are five, six or seven of these companies throughout the country in that same position, but that during the course of the year it is decided that for the advantage of the general public the number of these licenses should be reduced, even though these companies have made heavy expenditures. They

Supply-Marine and Fisheries-Radio
will have tio suffer the loss of their licenses; they have no claim against us; they have no vested right. Otherwise, if the contention of my hon. friend were sound, once a license is issued it would 'have to be renewed after a year and no one could think of refusing that renewal or of cancelling that license.
That is not the practice. I know what my hon. friend has in mind; the department is not supposed to do that without having some good reason, and I am quite ready to admit that fact; that is what I stated last night.
I contend that in this particular case we had reasons strong enough to justify our action. Hon. gentlemen do not agree with that, but it is a matter of judgment; if they do not agree with my decision they are free to have their own view in that regard.
May I ask the minister if he will give us the reasons of the government for taking this action? So far they have not been given, to my knowledge.

I do not see any necessity or any advantage in repeating again and again in this house or elsewhere statements which already have been made. I stated the reasons in my remarks to the house on April 12, and my statement will be found at page 1951 of Hansard. I repeat, those reasons may not be sufficient in the minds of certain members of the house or of certain people outside the house, but that is no reason for saying that I am to be blamed or censured because I have exercised the authority given me by the law and the regulations. My reasons may not be good; the loser in a law suit is not satisfied with the judgment, but he has lost his case just the same. I submit that our reasons were sufficient to justify our action; those reasons have been plainly stated in this house and they are to be found in greater detail in the documents which have been filed. I do not believe the minister who has the responsibility in regard to these matters can occupy a more sound position than to take care first of all of the listeners-in, and to look after the interest of the broadcasting stations after that. After all the public at large, the listeners-in, are to be considered first; the welfare, the benefit and the enjoyment of the mass of the population which is composed of the listeners-in should be considered beifore anything else. In the decision which we made we tried to satisfy the listeners-in, after hearing their representations and their protests.
I regret to say that it has been stated that I may have been induced, in giving that decision, to a<ct as a censor of religious beliefs or creeds. From that one may draw the inference that in dealing with the matters of
my department I am somewhat prejudiced from a religious point of view. I desire to state most emphatically that this is not the case; in dealing with the matters which come under my jurisdiction I try to be fair and just to everyone who has anything to do with tJhe affairs of my department. I may be lacking in many qualifications possessed by others both in and out of this house; I may not be so important as many others, but from the point of view of fairness, honesty, tolerance and sense of justice I have no leaves to take from the book of anyone in or out of this house. I may make mistakes; all men make mistakes, but I try to act with the greatest sense of justice, fairness and honesty towards all those who have dealings with my department, and I very much regret that certain inferences to the contrary may be drawn from remarks which have been made in this house.
The complaints upon which we acted came from three sources, as my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre said; complaints came from Toronto, from Saskatoon and from Vancouver.
Mr. 'SPENCER: May I ask the minister how many complaints came from Vancouver and Saskatoon?
I could not say offhand, but the number is stated in the papers tabled.
Three from the one place and six from the other, I believe.

My hon. friend may be
right. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre drew atention to a certain number of these complaints taken from the papers tabled, but I say that it was hardly fair to pick out a certain number of letters or complaints which might suit his argument and pass over other complaints which are of a general character. The complaints made are not confined to matters of religious belief, or creed, they are of a general character. One has only to look at the return which has been produced to ascertain that the complaints are of a general character. The complaints which have come from Vancouver, while they may not be numerous, have come from a representative association of people interested in radio broadcasting and in matters connected with that new industry and its development. The complaints received from Vancouver include a resolution adopted by the Greater Vancouver Radio Association, a body of listeners-in, and also one from the Radio Trades Association, representing firms and individuals dealing in radio apparatus. It may be that the complaints are not numerous, but

Supply-Marine and Fisheries-Radio
they represent those who are supposed to be most directly interested, because they are listeners in, or are engaged in the business of selling the necessary apparatus.
, Has the department received any complaints regarding other broadcasting stations?

Yes, there are complaints
received all through the year against other stations, but I am free to say that they were more numerous in this particular case

When complaints are
received, is it not the custom of the department to send an inspector around? You have inspectors in every city-you have one in Calgary-and when complaints are re ceived, do you send an inspector to that particular station to talk the matter over with them, and possibly warn them; did you do that in this case?

I would venture to say it
was done in this case. Complaints have been made, and I think they have been filed in the return, by the inspectors themselves.
Did the association meet the requests of the inspectors?

As I stated before, inspectors, who had previously favoured the issuing of a license to the International Bible Students Association, took an opposite view last year and said that we should not renew that license. They informed us they had been flooded with protests of all kinds from the population of the cities where they were operating. These letters accused the department of failing to instruct the inspectors to stop certain broadcasting, and to prevent certain people from doing what they were doing; we were accused of not doing what we should do for the protection of the listeners-in.
Did you notify the association regarding the material being sent out?
The association were perfectly aware of the situation.

It appears to me, in handling this matter-I admit the difficulty of it-that when information comes to the government that a broadcasting station is sending out material objectionable to a great many people the government should notify the particular company concerned.

The people who enjoy
broadcasting are more or less in communication with the government all through the

year. I am informed that they are in communication with the officers of the department. There is an instance of that in the case mentioned by the member for South Vancouver (Mr. Ladner), in his remarks on page 3645 of Hansard, as follows:
On the other hand, when the license was cancelled it will be observed that over twenty thousand letters expressing appreciation of the programs were forwarded to the Department of Marine and Fisheries and duly acknowledged.
These letters were forwarded to the Department of Marine and Fisheries in 1927. apparently following the complaints which had come from Toronto. The sending of these letters was apparently to combat the accusations which had been made against those responsible for the broadcasting programs. This shows that these people cannot plead ignorance and say they were not informed. My hon. friend said that 20,000 letters were sent to show that the listeners-in were satisfied with the broadcasting and desirous of keeping the station in operation, and that the criticisms were not justified.

Did the minister warn
these people that if they did not stop broadcasting objectionable matter their license would be cancelled; did he give them any warning at all of the premeditated action of the government?
I will frankly say, Mr. Chairman, that I have no recollection of any special warning having been sent to them.

Do you not think you
should have given them notice?

We informed them about
one month before its expiration that the license would not be renewed. I am quite free to confess that I have no remembrance of any special warning having been sent to them before that.

Is that not the custom,
with other broadcasting stations?

I will say that we have
never been placed in such an embarrassing position as we have in this case, and in connection with that I would express a wish which is very strong in my mind:	The
sooner I can get rid of this and have it taken out of the department, the better it will be for me. To say that they did not know of the complaints against them is not quite accurate. They knew the situation; they knew that complaints had been made and that we were forced to consider them in the interests of the listeners-in of Canada.

, Supply-Marine and Fisheries-Radio
The hon. member for Vancouver South is quite mistaken when he says that 20,000 letters expressing appreciation of the programs were forwarded to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Not 20.000 letters, but 5,029 letters in four packages were forwarded by the association to the department. Out of these 5,029 letters, 24 were complaints, and 5,005 were letters of commendation. But here is the interesting part; out of the 5,005 letters of commendation, 4,056 were from people living in the United States of America, and only 949 were from Canada. These were the supposed 20,000 letters forwarded to us in 1927 to answer the complaints which had been made against this association.

I would ask the minister
if there was not a clear and direct expression of opinion in the petitions which have been sent to the extent of 482,000 people?
I am coming to that.

I would also ask the
minister if he himself has not received a large number of letters, as most of us have from our constituents, on the subject?

I will come to that. Regarding the petitions which have been sent to the Prime Minister, it is stated that they contain about 458,026 names of which only 82,468 are those of persons who claim to be radio listeners.
Owners.

No, radio listeners. But
without saying anything against the people who have signed these petitions and for whom I have the greatest respect, I may say that everyone who has any experience in public life knows how easy it is to have a petition signed in regard to practically everything. Have we not all had in our experience a petition on which certain names would appear and the next morning the same names would appear on a petition asking exactly the contrary of what was asked in the previous one? We have all had that experience and it is not surprising that such a thing has been done. I do not blame people for doing that, but during the last month these people have been broadcasting to all their listeners that they ought to make strong representations that freedom of speech should not be done away with in Canada. I do not blame them in any way and I respect them, but in deciding the matter I have to take the situation as it is and to analyse the facts as they are. These people have had friends of theirs, no doubt acting in good faith, passing through the different communities with petitions and asking
people to sign them. There came to the department afterwards certain letters from people saying that they regretted having signed the petition because they did not know what was the matter and they were not given the full facts of the case. There is one instance of a boy of seven years who, in the absence of his parents, was asked to sign a petition to give back the license to the International Bible Students' Association. Another case was that of a maid who was asked to sign the petition although she said she did not know a single thing about the radio business; yet she was asked to sign the petition. I have numerous letters from people who signed under similar circumstances. I repeat that I do not blame them; they were acting in good faith, but this shows how easy it is to build up a petition and secure signatures. Supposing we sent persons to Toronto, or Vancouver, to ask people in those cities to sign petitions against the International Bible Students' Association. I venture to say we would be in a position to come before the house with a petition bearing at least as many names as the one which has been produced before us.
We are supposed to have received 9,358 letters in the department. The department has issued 267,210 licenses to listeners and the protests that we have received from people holding receiving licenses number 1,658. Out of 267,210 licensed listeners-in, we have received complaints or protests from only 1,658. We have not had time to analyse the petition containing the 458,026 names.

Is the minister not mistaken there? He referred a moment ago to the matter with regard to the 82,468. My information is that these state in their petition that they are owners of radio receiving sets and they make the protest.
The information which has been supplied to me by the officer of the department who has looked into these petitions is that out of 458026 names, 82,468 claim to be radio listeners.
Owners.
Listeners. That is the information I have before me.

May I take the liberty of suggesting-and I do so with all respect to freedom of speech and all the rest of it-that while there are in the house a few who are greatly interested in changing the minister's decision in this matter, I think the vast majority of us are satisfied to let the minister take the responsibility, which he has said he is willing to do, for the action he has taken,
3658	COMMONS
Supply-Marine and Fisheries-Radio
and endeavour to get on with the business of the house? The minister has taken straightforwardly and squarely upon his shoulders the responsibility of cutting off these people. I may say-and I say this subject to further study-that from what little I have studied of the situation I rather think the minister is right; but at any rate, irrespective of what I think about the matter, I believe the house at this late stage in the session could be far better occupied than in fighting out a question of this sort. If the minister is willing to take the responsibility, as he has said he is, let him be criticized by those who do not agree with him; but we have spent hours on this question and without meaning to reflect in any way upon any hon. gentlemen who may think differently from me, I wish to offer the suggestion that we would be better occupied in dealing with some of the real business of the house than in carrying on this particular question.

In view of the importance of the subject and the agitation that has been going on, I think it is proper that I should state clearly the position, first, for the government, and second for myself. I do not want to be accused, as I have been most unfairly in certain newspapers and elsewhere, of having been unjust and of having acted at the dictation of persons belonging to the church to which I belong. It is only fair that I be given an opportunity to make my statement and to place the whole facts before the committee. The facts have to a certain extent been presented but only from one side, and I should like to submit some information from our side of the problem in order to enable unprejudiced people to form their opinion. I quite agree with the hon. member for Fort William who has just spoken. This is not a matter which should, from a certain point of view, take the right of way over other business; but the question is so important and it has been given such wide publicity in the press and elsewhere that it is proper that I should answer the criticism advanced by members of the house who have expressed their views, I admit, in good faith, and in a very fair way-a way that I appreciate very much.
With respect to the action which the government has taken in regard to the numerous letters which were sent to the department, we have discovered that a great number of these letters are in the same handwriting, and that the only difference is in the signature. The letter had evidently been prepared in advance by somebody else, and was offered for signature to many people. The action of

the department has been approved in many communications which we have received. Many letters of congratulation and of felicitation have been addressed to the government on account of the action we took, and I may add that, generally speaking, the editorial sections of the newspapers throughout the country have approved of the action of the government in regard to this matter. So I think there is something to be said on my side, in support of the action taken by myself with the approval of the government.
We speak, and we hear very much, about the freedom of the air. I do not hesitate to say that the air is as free as it was before. But the use of the air has never been free, and so far as radio is concerned, the use of the air cannot be free, because if it were open to anyone to use the few channels of communication that we have in the radio service, the result would be chaos. This is a matter which has to be regulated and controlled for otherwise there is no liberty, and no advantage to anyone. If there is no regulation, if everybody is free to go on the air, then his neighbour should have the same privilege, and if they all go on the air together at the same time, using the same system, nobody would enjoy the air because there would be too much interference, and no one would get any benefit at all from radio broadcasting. So there can be no freedom in the use of the air. It has been controlled in all countries of the world. It is being controlled in the United States; it has been controlled and is being controlled in England to-day by the British Broadcast Corporation.
It must be remembered that we cannot appropriate to ourselves a certain number of wave-lengths for our own use. Others might use the same wave-length, and no satisfactory results would be obtained. I read not very long ago in a newspaper that it was very strange that the United States Should be controlling the wave-lengths, the channels of radio communication, and that we had simply to follow their decisions. That is not exactly the case. What would be the situation of Canada if we started to-day fighting with the United States, we operating our stations and they operating theirs? The result would be simply chaos, and no one would get any advantage from the broadcasting stations, and in addition, their strong stations would very easily drown out the stations we have in Canada. This is a matter which has to be adjusted by an understanding between the two countries, and that is the only way to deal with it. I have always understood that my freedom and my liberty stops where my neighbour's begins, and that I cannot invade

Supply-Marine and Fisheries-Radio
the path upon which my neighbour is travelling. I have to respect his rights as much as I expect him to respect mine.
Hon. gentlemen who have spoken already have spoken of the freedom of the air, but fredom only for the broadcasting people. I am for the freedom of the air in the interests of the listeners-in, first of all, and I think that no broadcasting station has any right, simply under the phrase "the freedom of the air'' to impose upon me or upon anybody else his convictions or opinions and to force me to listen to them the whole day or the whole night. That is the position.

Why should the
minister rule these people out entirely, and then grant a license, for instance, to Gooder-ham and Worts to broadcast whiskey advertisements.

I have already given my
reasons for that. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre may think they are no good; that is his privilege, but I think my reasons are good.

The way it appears to me now, in the light of the great number of persons who have petitioned against this action, is that the attitude and action of the government have been rather strict, having regard to the fact that the bookstalls in this city of Ottawa and all over the province of Ontario are loaded with American literature which cannot be regarded as having anything but a damaging effect on the young people of this Dominion. It seems to me that there is a good deal of laxity in regard to United States literature coming into this country, and in view of this laxity the

Supply-Marine and Fisheries-Radio
action of the government in regard to cancelling this radio license does appear somewhat severe.
I have received, as have other hon. members, a number of letters in regard to the cancellation of this license. I have talked with a good many people who have sets of their own, and I have asked them if they have ever heard anything which struck them as improper being issued by this society, and in not a single instance did anyone tell me that they had heard anything which they thought was objectionable. That is all I have to go on in forming my opinions, in the absence of a definite statement as to the sort of stuff this organization has been broadcasting. If the minister has that information and does not care to place it on Hansard, I should be glad if he would make it available for me and other members of parliament to glance over it, so that we can form our own judgment as to the real character of the matter which has been broadcast, and about which the minister has received some complaints.
Certainly, I will.

I have no desire to prolong the discussion at this stage, because anything I might add would be more or less a repetition of things which have already been said. However, there is one point I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and it grows out of the discussion last night just prior to the adjournment of the house. Just before the moment of adjourning the house at eleven o'clock last night, I had stated that there were complaints in the correspondence brought down for the year 1918 and 1919. The minister said he thought I was mistaken. I went to the trouble to-day to obtain the correspondence tabled, and I find that my statement was correct. Before placing the facts before the house I would like to preface my remarks with an observation or two. On April 16, the house passed the following resolution:
For a copy of all letters, telegrams, and correspondence, pertaining to the cancellation of the radio licenses held by the International Bible Students' Association.
The correspondence asked for in this resolution was brought down on the 7th of May, exactly three weeks after the motion for the production of these papers was passed. At the time this motion was passed by the house it was understood, I believe, and was so stated by the right hon. the Prime Minister, that only correspondence would be produced .hat pertained to the cancellation of these licenses. That is all we wanted, and I believe that that
56103-232*
is all that was asked for. But when the correspondence was produced, this is what I find.
In the first place, there is a letter sent from the Department of Marine and Fisheries, dated the 12th of April, when the motion, I believe, was already on the order paper, practically asking for information against the International Bible students. A letter came back on the 17th day of April. I find also several other letters on this file dated about the same period. In other words, the department cancelled the licenses, and after they had done so, they looked around for evidence to justify them in taking their action. I do not think that is fair; it is not the kind of action we should care to justify in this house.
I look towards the end of this file of correspondence and I find articles reproduced from the American newspapers of about the year 1918. There is one dated March 8, 1918, and these are given, I presume, as a reason for the cancellation of these licenses. It is quite true that there may have been many people in 1917 or 1918 who might have agreed with the action then taken against the Bible students in Toronto or New York, but certainly that is no excuse to be given to this house in the year 1928 for the cancellation of these licenses. I think it is a most unfair thing, and I believe that it is not in keeping with the traditions of this house, when we ask for correspondence pertaining to a certain action, that after the date of asking for the correspondence the department should go around looking for correspondence to table. The only reason I got up this afternoon was to protest against this method of the department, and to protest also against going back for a period of ten years for evidence against this association. In 1918 and 1919 there was no such thing as a radio license granted by the Department of Marine and Fisheries in Canada. I believe it was only in 1920 or 1921 that licenses were first granted by the government. It is unjust to this association that these matters should be brought to the attention of the house, and what is more, I do not think it is becoming the government to go around looking for evidence after a motion is passed by the house. What I mean by that is this. After I had asked on the 16th of April for the tabling of the correspondence pertaining to the cancellation of these licenses, the government go around to the various departments, such as the Post Office department, and to newspaper offices probably, and clip items out of newspapers and paste them in the record, and then table it all to justify their action. That is the protest I wish to make this afternoon.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries-Radio

The documents which have been produced at the request of my hon. friend are all the documents existing on the file of the department regarding this association. We thought it would be fair to place before the house everything that we had relating to this association. The documents to which my hon. friend has just referred were taken into consideration, I am informed by the officers of the department, when the International Bible students made their first request for a radio license in 1922, which request was refused at the time, and I am told that the request was refused at that time on the strength of the documents to which my bon. friend has just referred. When we brought down the correspondence, we wanted to bring down everything in our possession with regard to the matter.

May I point out that this document is dated April 17, 1928, which is after the license had been cancelled, and consequently the statement of the minister has no bearing on this communication to which I have referred.

I have just a few
words to say in respect to the matter that is before the house. The minister has done something which a great many people are condemning him for, and yet perhaps some of those who are condemning him find themselves in the same position as I do myself, of rather feeling that he has done a service to a great many people in the country. I do not wish to discuss at length the religious teaching of the Bible students, but I do wish to point out that a great many people throughout the country share the opinion that their teaching was not wholesome and was not welcome. Our population is made up of various religious sects. I find that 96 per cent of our people belong to religious bodies that certainly do not accept the religious teaching of the International Bible Students; for instance, the Anglicans, the Baptists, the Brethren, the Con-gregationalists, the Evangelical Association, the Friends-known as the Quakers-the Lutherans, the Mennonites, the Methodists, the Plymouth Brethren, the Presbyterians, the Roman Catholics, the Salvation Army, and several others composing approximately 96 per cent, or over eight million of our population. These people in general do not accept the religious teaching of the International Bible Students' Association, because their doctrine is so different from that of the majority of our religious organizations that it is not acceptable to them. Therefore I find myself in the position of commending the minister for the stand he has taken.
[Mr. Heaps.l
The argument has been advanced that his action constitutes interference with liberty of speech. Well, I am not so sure that it does. "Liberty of speech" is a phrase capable of a variety of meanings. We have liberty of speech in some matters, in others we have not. Even in the manner of speaking our thoughts we are restrained to quite an extent-especially in this chamber. Here we are not permitted, for instance, to make any derogatory remarks about the sovereign, or the governor general, or even about the upper chamber.

Or even about each other,
much as we should like to.
Quite so. We think a lot more than we say, and under our breath we may muttei; comments that we should not like to appear on Hansard.
Hear, hear.
Order.

While the Bible
students are forbidden to give forth their religious teaching on the air, they still have the medium of the pulpit. They are not restrained in the least from using that channel. Also, they still have the privilege of going into our homes-which, 'by the way, they do very aggressively-and trying to sell their literature; and they still have the privilege, to use a slang phrase, of buttonholing people on the train or in the street, which also they are very aggressive in doing. In short, they are not restrained in these respects from disseminating their views, so I do not feel that any great injustice is done them so far as liberty of speech goes.
There is, though, room for criticism in another particular. I feel the minister is sub-j ect to some degree of criticism because of discrimination. Yesterday we learned that the United Church of Canada has a broadcasting station in Vancouver, and that the Christian and Missionary Alliance has a broadcasting station in Edmonton. I know something of the latter because I was concerned in getting it there. The International Bible Students used to have four broadcasting stations. Now I think there is discrimination in that the licenses for the four stations of the Bible students were cancelled, while these other two religious stations had their licenses renewed. I do not know whether I should suggest how that discrimination might be overcome, but I should like to give forth a thought that was expressed to me last night by a minister of the Gospel in this city-one who, I believe, has charge of the largest congregation locally. He told me that he would favour discontinuing the broadcasting of all

Supply-
-Marine and Fisheries-Radio
religious programs. Now, if the minister had taken that attitude and refused to license the broadcasting station of any religious organization, his position would be unassailable. 1 believe there is something to 'be said in support of the view that the broadcasting of any religious programs should not be permitted. The attitude of this reverend gentleman of course was taken because in his opinion such broadcasting tends to keep people away from church, where he thinks they should attend. So he may be selfish in his opinion.
A point that has not been brought out in this discussion is that the International Bible Students Association have really had a special privilege.
Hear, hear.

I am not very conversant with their programs other than those broadcast from their Saskatoon station. If my information is correct, they enjoyed a special privilege there in this way: they operated t'heir own station, and in addition they had a certain amount of time for broadcasting from another local station. The Ministerial Association of Saskatoon met together and allotted the time that each denomination would have for broadcasting, leaving the Bible students out of consideration as they had their own stations for their exclusive use. But afterwards the Ministerial Association was approached by the Bible students, who said: Here, we wish for our share of the time with the other religious bodies on your station. And they were legally entitled ito their share, and got it. So they had all their time on their own station, and their share with the other religious bodies of the broadcasting on the joint station.

What about freedom of
speech?

They had an excess of freedom of speech-an excess of time. Now that the department has refused to renew the Bible students' license for their station they are on a parity with the other religious organizations in Saskatoon. So instead of their being discriminated against, I feel that their special privileges have been withdrawn and they are now simply put on a par with the other religious bodies, where they should have been from the first.
I was pleased to note the minister's statement that the government proposes to take over the control of radio. I think that is the proper policy to adopt, and I do not think it is necessary to spend very much money or consume a great deal of time in order to arrive at a sound decision. In my opinion the
government should take over radio broadcasting as a public business and direct it in the interests of the whole country.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make it clear that I hold no brief for the Bible students against the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I do not think it necessary to attribute any ulterior motives to the minister or to the government in this matter. I think his refutation of the charge of ulterior motives was both dignified and convincing, at least so far as I was concerned. I believe that the minister, as he Aimed, had a perfect right to form his opinion on the evidence given. At the same time I think he will concede to others the right to estimate the value of his opinion. Personally I believe that the minister's action was somewhat precipitate; he did not have regard to principles that are traditional and that lie very deep at the root of our most valued and cherished beliefs. This year we are celebrating the third centenary of John Bunyatn. The whole Englishspeaking world is looking back with pride upon the record of tfhat humble English tinker, not because he produced one of England's premier classics, which is the next best seller to the Bible, but because he spent twelve long years in prison to maintain the right of free speech. I say these matters go much deeper than we perceive on the surface, and a good many of us, no matter what our relationship to the Bible students may be, are very intensely interested in the question of free speech, the freedom of religious opinion and the freedom to express that opinion.
It seems to me, from what has been said, that the objections to the Bible students in this phase of their propaganda have come mainly from three classes of the community, to whom I do not think we ought to give undue weight. First of all there are those who are antipathetic to the religious views of the Bible students. It has been said that the Bible students are propagandists; they have been stigmatized with that as though it is something to be condemned. I put it to the house, that to be a propagandist in religious matters is not a thing that bears with it any stigma at all. After all, looking back on the history of religious controversy, it has been the propagandists who have made their mark in the progress of religion, notwithstanding what their religious views have been. I do not agree with the theological beliefs of this sect; they are not beliefs that I can accept. But that is a very secondary matter. At any rate these people, whatever their views are, believe in them enough to go to some trouble to try to disseminate them amongst Cana*
3670	COMMONS
Supply-Marine and Fisheries-Radio
dians; and in my view the dissemination of religious beliefs in contemporary life is not by any means overdone. It seems to me that the ideas that are coursing through the minds and hearts of the people are not ideas that are overburdened with religious conceptions of any kind. After all, I admire any people, Mohammedans or Christians or whatnot, who show some zeal in the prosecution and spread of their religious beliefs. And1 many of us know these Bible students personally; they are our neighbours. There is scarcely a town or hamlet in western Canada where some of these people do not reside. They are amongst our best Canadian citizens; they can be classified as the very best of our Canadian citizens. I understand that they do not believe very much in us politicians. Their kingdom is not of this world; therefore they do not lay much stress upon the achievements of worldly institutions. I do- not know whether we can hold that against them or not; a good many of us have become pessimistic about the efficacy of some of our institutions.

Can the hon.
member assure the house whether or not they believe in rendering to Caesar the things that are Caesar's?

I think that the people who
raise that question ought to be sure that they are rendering unto God the things that are God's. The onus is on the other people, not on the Bible students. I am not holding any brief for the other-worldly conceptions of these people. But they are not the only religious sect that have been other-worldly in their beliefs.
Another set of objections come from people who are very patriotic. They believe that the sect is a menace to the country; that its teachings somewhat blur the lines of nationalism; in other words, that they are not very patriotic, and that during the war they were anti-militaristic. I will not tax the religious knowledge of my fellow members, but I want to ask hon. members, who have any knowledge of religious history, to tell me of any sect which at its best time was not anti-nationalist and anti-militarist. I could wait for the reply with perfect confidence that no satisfactory answer can be given to that question, because it is well known that in the case of religious sects that bear the name Christian-and this sect does-the more sincere they are, the more nearly they get back to the first principles of their belief, the more antipathetic and antagonistic they become to all conceptions of a narrow, Chauvinistic, nationalist spirit and to all ideas of military aggressiveness. You can-

not name one of the great Orthodox churches, let alone this little modem sect, of which this is not true. One remembers that away back in the sixteenth century Sir Thomas More, who, as a faithful Catholic, suffered' for his belief in transubstantiation, was a pacifist, just as these people are to-day-an associate of Henry the VIII who in his younger days was known by his pacifism. And these people were pacifists because they believed that it was the teaching of Jerome and of St. Augustine, and indeed of Paul and of Christ himself. I think therefore that we ought to hesitate before branding a modern sect because it enunciates beliefs of a pacifistic character. I think any sect to-day which has the courage to come out in this materialistic age and enunciate beliefs of a pacifistic kind bears the marks of the true church in a way that some of our more orthodox churches have not borne it in recent -times. I think that is a very far-fetched objection to this sect.

I do not claim to be an
authority on religion, but just for the sake of information who was it said:
Think not that I am come to send peace on earth; I came not to send peace, but a sword.
A member of my hon.,friend's race said that.
Who was it?

I have followed this debate with perhaps a good deal of selfish interest, as I have a great many of these people in
3672^	COMMONS
Supply-Marine and Fisheries-Radio
my constituency. I have received many communications protesting against the action of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I desire to associate myself with the Iasi speaker .in that I do not accuse the minister of anything ulterior in this matter, but I believe he is a victim of a blunder on the part of the officials in his department; I say that frankly, I do not think the action was wholly warranted; I do not think the reasons given to the house are such as we should be expected to accept. For these reasons I hope that before this vote passes the minister will state to the house that he will have an investigation made, and if there is discrimination he will have it removed. It has been stated by hon. members that there is discrimination, and that belief is not wholly removed from my mind. It will make it very much easier for a lot of us if the minister will make such a statement, and I hope he does so before the vote passes.

Of all the criticism which has been made from both sides of the house with regard to the minister's action I believe the most biting was made by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary), when he pointed out that the station CJYC Was cancelled' to make room for others, including OFCA. I should like to know whether the minister can give us an explanation of the action of his department in this respect. Does he question the statement made by the hon. member for South Toronto?
Mr. Chairman, I deny that imputation. The license of the International Bible Students' Association, or of the Universal Radio of Canada, was not cancelled to favour any other station.

Probably I should say
that the license was not renewed?

That is not the reason.
There is no connection between what is supposed to be favoritism, according to my hon. friend opposite, and the action taken in this particular case.

Considering the answer given by the minister to my question this afternoon, that he had not warned these people, would he consider regranting their license on condition that they did not broadcast anything of an offensive nature?
You do not look like that in your picture.

I think I answered that
point when I said that no special warning or notice was given before refusing to renew the license. I stated that they were absolutely

familiar with the situation as it existed; they knew of the complaints we had received against them, one of the indications of that being that they sent to the department a certain number of letters.
It is the latter part of my question I am more particularly interested in. Would the minister be willing to grant them a trial license, say for a month?
I can only say that an investigation is to be held into the whole situation, and I am ready to place the case of the Universal Radio station before the commission.

Item agreed to.
Marine department-river St. Lawrence ship channel-maintenance and operating dredging fleet, $1,895,000.

This is the annual vote for the dredging of the St. Lawrence channel from Montreal to Father Point. There is an increase of $373,000 to provide for the reconditioning of certain dredges which are getting old, and rebuilding one or two of them.
Is the usual annual vote about this size?
Yes.
Could you give us some idea as to the progress being made in dredging this channel?

The channel from Montreal to Father Point is 30 feet deep at certain points, and we have to dredge a distance of 34 miles before the program of deepening the channel to 36 feet is completed. We expect that it will take five or six years to complete this work.
Is that below Quebec?
Part is below Quebec and part above.

The channel has not a depth
of 35 feet below Quebec?
Not at all points.
I concluded from the remarks of the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) that there was nothing to be done there at all.
There is some dredging to be done.

What will be the ultimate cost?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

We are spending about
$1,800,000 per year, and there will be the same expenditure for five or six years.
About that, yes.

Item agreed to.
River St. Lawrence ship channel [DOT]- for construction of one hopper barge, $315,000.
Would the minister explain, please?
The Department of Railways and Canals being in need of a barge for their work in the Hudson bay, we lent them one, and this is to replace it.

Who is constructing the
barge?
It is being done by tender.
The lowest tenderer will get the work?
Oh, yes.

Item agreed to.
To provide for maintenance and operation of Sorel shipyard, $154,000.
Would the minister explain?
This amount is required for the maintenance and operating of the government shipyard in Sorel, where dredges and tugs used in dredging the St. Lawrence are repaired.

Item agreed to.
To provide for the construction of a regulating and retaining dams in the St. Lawrence river, $1,000,000

Will the minister explain
this item?

A few years ago a commission composed of engineers was placed in charge of the work of studying the problem of regulating the water in the St. Lawrence river from Montreal down to Father Point. This commission, which was composed of Mr. E. E. Haskell, Dean of the College of Civil Engineering, Cornell University; Mr. V. W. Forneret, Superintending Engineer of the St. Lawrence ship channel, and Mr. William J. Stewart, Hvdrographer of the Naval Service, who has died since that time, made a study with a view of raising the water more particularly in the harbour of Montreal. They caime to the conclusion that by the construction of some submerged dams in the St. Lawrence at certain points they could maintain the water at a higher level in the port of Montreal. It was suggested that submerged dams be established, one in lake St. Peter in the vicinity of Three Rivers, another one to unite the islands at the head of lake St. Peter in the vicinity of Sorel, about forty-five miles below Montreal, and a third a few miles below the port of Montreal. These engineers contended that with these submerged dams we could increase the depth of the water in the harbour of Montreal by nearly two feet and assure that depth throughout the year. That is the object of the expenditure.
Has the contract been let, and, if so, to whom?
No. Nothing has yet been done.
Tenders will be called for in the usual manner?
Yes.

Will this amount of a
million dollars be spent this year?
I am not sure but we may be placed in a position to give the contract for the whole thing.

What will be the total
cost?
In the vicinity of a million dollars.
That will cover the whole thing.
Yes.

What depth will these
submerged dams be below the water level?

That depends upon the level of the water at different periods of the year, but generally speaking I think there will be about two or three feet of water above them at low water to avoid any danger from the ice in the spring.	When the ice leaves
the St. Lawrence in the spring the water rises, but in the summer these dams will be submerged and there will be about two feet of water above them.
I presume they will be built on either side of the channel?

They will not be in the
channel in any way. They will be built from the shore to a certain distance towards the centre of the river to create obstructions to the flow of water in order to bring the water back into the port of Montreal. We do not propose to dam the St. Lawrence.

In regard to item 217
"River St. Lawrence ship channel-for construction of one hopper barge", the minister

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
gave an answer which seemed a little strange at the time. The minister mentioned the Hudson bay. The item speaks about the river St. Lawrence ship channel.

We lent the barge to the
Department of Railways and Canals.

To be used in Hudson
bay?
Yes. It is already there.
I understand the purpose of these dams is to retard the outflow of the water below Montreal.
Yes.

Is it intended to build
all three dams simultaneously, or one at a time? If the latter, which dam does the minister propose to build first?
The engineers of the department are working on that problem, but the indication is that they will start in the vicinity of Montreal.
Has the minister information in regard to the experience in other parts of the world on the subject?

I will frankly say I have
not that experience, but the engineers who prepared the report have, I think, procured information from other sources. I am sure they inquired about the possibilities or practicabilities of such a scheme. A report has been prepared by the commission. I am not sure that it was not tabled some years ago. I shall be pleased to supply a copy of it to my hon. friend.

Item agreed to.
Lighthouse and coast service - salaries and allowances to lightkeepers, $750,000.

I have just a question to ask the minister in connection with Mr. Dube, lighthouse keeper at Brandy Pot. I should like to know if there are different grades for lighthouse keepers and, if so, in what grade he is.

I regret very much that I am not in a position to give the information to my hon. friend at present. I have a great deal of information before me, but unfortunately, as often happens, the information asked for is not at hand. I shall be pleased to supply the information to my hon. friend.

Who compose the board
that looks after the grading of lighthouse keepers?

The members of the lighthouse board are the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the chief engineer of the

department, the commissioner of lights, the director of pilotage, Mr. Forneret, superintending engineer of the St. Lawrence ship channel,
a representative of the shipping federation, and also a representative of the Dominion Marine Association.
What is the quorum?

Generally speaking they are all there when there is a meeting, because practically all are officers of the department. There is, in addition, only the representative of the shipping federation and of the Dominion Marine Association.
Do they meet very often?

Requests come in to us for the establishment of lighthouses, and when we have a sufficient number of these representations we call a meeting of the lights house board. There is no stated time for its sittings. The board meets when there are sufficient representations to 'be dealt with.

I should like to say a few words on behalf of that lighthouse keeper, whom the Minister of Justice in this house knows very well. Brandy Pot island is not far from Hare island, in the middle of the St. Lawrence river, just in front of Riviere du Loup between the counties of Temiscouata and Charlevoix-iSaguenay. The river is very wide, some twelve to fourteen miles, at that point. This lighthouse is of the utmost importance to oceanic shipping. These vessels take their direction from that (lighthouse when they go up and down the river. I am very well acquainted with the lighthouse keeper, who has been there for several years, and not only does he perform his duties very efficiently, but in addition, he has performed a great deal of other work for the Department of Marine and Fisheries, in that he is a carpenter and has made all the repairs to the lighthouse with his own hands; so I do not think that it 'has cost the Department of Marine and Fisheries or the Department of Public Works very much for repairs to that lighthouse. That -is the first point.
The second point is this, that that light is of the utmost importance to every steamship and -sailing vessel in the -St. Lawrence river. There are some very dangerous reefs on the east side of the -island, and the light is, of course, of the greatest importance. There is another reason why that light is important, -and that is because there is not far from the lighthouse a very good harbour where sailing vessels can take shelter in bad weather.
There is another consideration which I wish to submit to the committee, and that is that

London and Port Burwell Railway
the lighthouse keeper is kept at his station, because of ice, sometimes as late as New Year's, and this year he had to stay there until the middle of January. Then he was taken off by the Montcalm and deft at Sydney, Cape Breton, and had to come on home from there. For these reasons I am asking for an increase of salary for this lighthouse keeper, and that he be put in a class with the other lighthouse keepers occupying important positions and carrying on very important duties. I hope the minister will have a kind word to say.

I will see if he can be given more favourable consideration.
Item stands.

maintopic: EDMONTON, DUNVEGAN AND BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish
to take this opportunity on the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), not to oppose any development of railways in British Columbia, but to place on Hansard certain resolutions which I have received. In order that I may do so adequately I shall ask hon. members to bear with me while I express myself in my mother tongue.
(Translation):	Mr. Chairman, I am delighted in being able to address the house on the subject of railways. In no way am I opposed to the expansion of railways, however, the question is sufficiently important for the committee to again discuss the bill submitted to the house, so as to avoid any possible error. If I mention any possible error,

Edmonton, Dunvegan Railway
it is because just recently the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) himself stated to this committee that he was not in a position to furnish us with certain information which consequently led to an adjournment of the debate and placed the responsibility on the hon. member for a fair share of the delay which this bill must undergo. The hon. member for Elgin West (Mr. Hep-bum) speaking in the house on May 4 last, stated that this measure should be the object of further study, and my opinion is, that this committee should earnestly take up its study and if necessary refer it back to the select standing committee on railways. The fact that this line is a private enterprise should make us the more cautious. Generally, these companies, after meeting with a certain amount of disappointment, appeal to the government for subsidies, then a few years later when they have squeezed out of the line every possible profit, they cease operations, it is then that the government are forced to operate the railway at their own expense, if they cannot find a responsible company to take the line- over. Here is an example of what I am asserting: in 1925 a railway company in my own riding was operating a line; after obtaining from the government many thousands of dollars and having squeezed out all possible profits from the enterprise, the company ceased operations, and I was obliged to earnestly request the government to take the necessary means to continue operating this line. While on the subject, I wish to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), also the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), and a number of my colleagues, who gave me their strong support at the time. Thanks to the government, expropriation proceedings were taken before the exchequer court and the line was purchased by the Canadian National; a few months later it was resold to the Canadian Pacific which, to-day, is operating the line, and I hope will soon realize very handsome profits. However, there is still a portion of this line which is not operated. I trust that this powerful company so admirably managed, not only in the province I reside in, but throughout the whole country, will find it possible to put into operation that part of the railway so as to link it with the Maine Central, on the United States side. My constituents are anxious to see the whole of this line operated not only for the advantage it may bring to my county, but so that the beautiful province of Quebec may have its due share of railways and compare favourably with other provinces.
Recently, sir, the newspapers of Edmonton, and among these the Edmonton Bulletin, reported that the Hon. Vernon W. Smith, Minister of Railways in the province of Alberta, had expressed his astonishment to hear that this measure, sponsored by the hon. member for Peace River, met with such strong opposition on the part of the eastern members. I wish to convey to the Hon. Mr. Smith the assurance that we are greatly interested in the development and prosperity of that vast region of the Peace River, to which this bill refers. However, I shall take the opportunity which the remarks of the Hon. Mr. Smith afford me, to state that if the people of the Peace River region wish to obtain certain railway development, they should warn their representatives to be more indulgent towards the members on the right, when they bring up measures m the interest of the people not only of the province of Quebec but of the whole Dominion. There is a proverb which says: Give and you shall receive. The hon. member for Peace River was unable to surround himslf with friends who would have been well disposed to reciprocate the help he might have extended in the development of railways in the other provinces.
The people of certain counties in the eastern townships, as well as those of Richelieu, Yamaska and Drummond have for ever so long requested! the construction of a railway. The representatives of these ridings would be very pleased if they could obtain this railway so long expected, and which would be advantageous not only to those counties but to the greater portion of the eastern townships. Instead of receiving their goods by way of Montreal, the manufacturers and the public as a whole would be served by this line. They could forward their goods through the port of Sorel and at less expense if this railway was built. I have received resolutions from various boards of trade appealing to the government in this matter.
A few years ago the member for Matane introduced a bill bearing the No. 24. An Act incorporating the Pabos, Amqui and Edmund-ston, Railway Company, it was given its first reading on March 22, 1920, however this railway was not approved of.
Mr. Chairman, I trust this committee will not refuse to listen for a few moments to the reading of the request lately made by the Board of Trade of Amqui with reference to the Gaspe peninsula:
The Grspe peninsula has reached the turning point is ts history; it is said, that it is on the eve of being rediscovered. And it is not too soon. At the time of the discovery of the new world, European navigators were continously seeking a passage to India and sailed towards

Edmonton, Dunvegan Railway
the west, coming to a stop, after they had found out their mistake, this accounts for the interior of the country being settled before the coast which nevertheless is nearer to the old continent.
No doubt the Gaspe peninsula is rich enough in natural resources and sufficiently picturesque to draw one's attention; but we are living in an epoch when merit is not always acknowledged, and that is why it is sometimes necessary to make a little fuss over a name. The Board of Trade therefore wishes to do its bit.
While the Gaspe boundaries do not extend as far as Montmagny, it is not the less almost a province, six times as large as Prince Edward Island. Experts contend that its territory comprises 70,000,000 cords of pulpwood; engineers find that there is place for the settlement of about fifty parishes; its soil is of the best and well watered; there are sufficient water powers for the needs of the region; fisheries exist which can compare favourably with the finest in the world. Within the last few years mines, of inexhaustible wealth have been discovered. We do not wish to mention its natural beauties, its picturesque landscapes which attract tourists from all parts, as we especially wish to interest business people. Owing to its geographical situation, Gaspd is the part of the country nearest to Europe, by about 300 miles; Gaspe, with railway facilities to Montreal and the western cities by way of Amqui, is nearer by again 300 miles or more, to the large centres than is any other port on this side of the Atlantic, Notwithstanding all these advantages, the Gaspe peninsula up to the present time has been considered of little importance. Means of communication are lacking, its population must depend on its local resources, the young people must seek work elsewhere.
What is the remedy to all these ills? A railway, a line linking Gaspe to Amqui and connecting with the National Railways.
The development of the country, the progress of industry require that ports be build for the export of our products; Halifax and Hudson Bay will not suffice, and there are on the Gaspe coast at least six ports which can be improved, at a low cost, and become winter ports.
We think that our turn has come to be placed on the same footing as the other parts of the country, and we humbly request the governments at Ottawa and Quebec not to forget the Gaspe peninsula, nor always neglect it as it has been the case up to the present time.
The interest of the whole country demands it. ifmqui, February, 1928.
Other resolutions have been presented. I think they are of the utmost importance as this honourable house will shortly ascertain.
We learn through the newspapers that within the last few years the Gaspe people have been asking for the construction of a railway, looked upon as a necessity to insure the future of this vast region, the area of which covers about 12,000 square miles-most of which forming a plateau of very rich arable land covered with timber which cannot be got out by utilizing the rivers, the sub-soil is highly mineralized: lead, zinc, silver, copper and 
gold are to be found, as it has been shown by prospecting and mining operations undertaken within the last ten years. In his 1927 report, Mr. F. J. Alcock, official geologist of the Canadian government expresses himself as follows:	To the geological viewpoint, the
interior of Gaspe offers very attractive prospects. ''The discovery of a number of veins has abundantly shown the richness of these mineral deposits. However, it is difficult to travel in that region; there are very few roads and they are rather in poor condition. The provincial government has already done a great deal for the mining development of that region by assisting in the construction of highways". It is this Gaspe plateau extending in length for 150 miles which we are seeking to open up to settlement, mining and timber development, and, at the same time, further the ends of agriculture. It is with this object in view that we request the immediate construction of a railway through the interior of the Gaspe peninsula. This is requested both in the town of Gaspe and at the other extremity of the peninsula, that is in the upper part of the Matapedia valley. It was also the desire expressed by the member for Matane (Mr. Dionne) when, speaking on the budget in this House, on February 21, 1928, he requested the construction, of that railway which he designated by the name that indicates its lay out, the Gaspe Matapedia Edmundston Railway. We beseech all members to support the request of the hon. member for Matane, a request made to the hon Minister of Railways, also communicated to the cabinet ministers representing that district of Quebec, as well as to members more directly interested in this project. This request was simultaneously made by both the Boards of Trade of Amqui and Sayabec. We estimate that the construction of the Gaspe-Matapedia portion, which is the most pressing one to-day, would cost between seven and eight million dollars. We beseech our colleagues to consider the railway situation of Canada as a whole. Even after receiving the grant of these $8,000,000 for that section of our province there cannot possibly be any fear that we shall have received more than our fair share. Let us, to be more brief and clear, divide the country in four sections and with the help of Canada's official statistics for 1926, let us endeavour to discover what important part each section plays, what is the share of each in railway mileage, what traffic each section supplies to feed these railways, and what would

According to the figures stated we can conclude as follows: 1st the Prairie section with a territory slightly larger than that of Quebec and a slightly smaller population has 16,561 miles of railway; 2nd the four maritime provinces with a population more than 30 per cent inferior to that of Quebec, have 7,755 miles, while Quebec's share is but 4,797 miles, which is too little if we consider its size, population and value as a national asset. Yet, Quebec and Ontario, the two oldest provinces of Canada, paid in 1925-1926 $146,722,230, for the	administration	of the
country, railways included, they have both together but 15,707 miles of railway. The other seven provinces pay only $42,215,245 and have 24,316 miles of railway. Note that the amount paid by Ontario is $88,724,249, and that paid by Quebec is $57,997,981.
A fair distribution of railways between the four Canadian sections should take place according to their respective population, that Is in a ratio of 47 miles per 10,000 people; the Maritime and British Columbia provinces would have 7,538 instead of 7,755 miles; the Prairie provinces 10,247 instead of 16,561 miles; Ontario 14,781 instead of 10,908 miles; and Quebec's share would be 11,096 instead of
4,796 miles. Therefore the Maritime section has 217 miles more than its share and the Prairies 6,314 miles; while Ontario would be entitled to 3,873 miles more, and Quebec to also 6,299 more. That was the situation as it existed two years ago. Since then new railways have been under construction, always in the West. The 1928 program includes four important new branches. We do not contend that the west has too many lines, but that Quebec has not enough. If the Quebec members show a sense of generosity in promoting the general welfare of the country and of the west especially, even though they practically control the administration by their numbers, they expect in return the no less generous co-operation of all the members outside of Quebec, when it is a question of carrying out necessary work for the normal progress of their province and the country as a whole. It is an easy matter to show that Quebec suffers from the lack of railway transportation. Its normal expansion in connection with agricultural and industrial progress is greatly impeded by it. The rural population, weary of the isolation caused by the great distances which separate it from transportation lines in order to reach the

Edmonton, Dunvegan Railway
markets where its products are sold, desert the farm for the cities, or else emigrates to the United States where living conditions seem to be easier. We must therefore conclude that we need more railways in Quebec. The most remote parts are those that have the greatest need of them and the Gaspe peninsula especially suffers from this lack of railways; it requests the construction of this railway which will link Gaspe, through its interior, to the Matapedia valley. Practically, this railway will cross almost in a bee line from Gaspe to Sayabec along the heights of the plateau and the heads of rivers. The reasons which seem to point to Sayabec, as the terminus for this first branch line are the following:	the Canadian National Railway has already at Sayabec extensive yards with a capacity for 400 cars, scales to weigh cars, a "Y" to turn the locomotives around and a shunter is in daily use. It is the locality of the Matapedia valley which at present supplies the most traffic to the National railway. There are extensive level grounds for the construction of the necessary shops for a terminus. If later on the traffic needs a further extension to Edmundston, New Brunswick; there is a natural pass at Sayabec on the same level as the present railway that will facilitate the crossing of the mountains which seem to block the way everywhere else.
Considering our position in the Dominion relatively to the other parts of the country, we are perfectly warranted in requesting this 150 miles of railway as part of what is due to us. We feel confident that we can depend upon this spirit of fairness and patriotism which animates all federal members, also upon the zeal of the Quebec members for the population they represent, as well as the impartial devotion of the members of the government in order to insure the construction of the Gaspe railway in a near future.
In closing my remarks, Sir, I wish simply to add that the hon. Minister of Railways is certainly deserving of our congratulations for what he has accomplished in the past, and I feel certain that, as well as the government, he desires the expansion of our railways not only in our beautiful province of Quebec, but equally throughout all the provinces which make up Canada.

I understand that when this bill was up some nights ago doubt was expressed as to who was asking for the legislation. There is am application to the Alberta government for a charter to enable the government to construct a railway to serve a settlement which is about fifteen years old and
[Mr Letellier.]
in which there has been produced in the last two years something like 2 million bushels of wheat. The settlers are farming from fifteen to ninety miles from a railway. I do not intend to ask that the bill be reported; I do not want to see anyone move the previous question. I want to make that explanation, and if anyone wishes to block the bill he is at liberty to do so and to take the responsibility.
iMr. SYLVESTTRE (Translation):	Mr. Chairman, when this bill was under consideration on May 4, last, I was unable to complete the remarks that I wished to make, as the time allotted for private bills had expired. To-night I want to complete them.
Considering that there are quite a number of French-Canadians settled in the region of the Peace River, I am sure that the sponsor of Bill No. 57 (Mr. Kennedy) must be pleased of the interest we display in this measure. Let us first examine clause 2 of the bill. It reads as follows:
The Company way within two years from the date of the passing of this Act commence to construct the lines of railway authorized by section one of this Act, and may within five years of the said date, complete the said lines of railway; and, if within the said periods respectively, the said lines are not commenced or are not completed and put in operation, the powers of construction conferred upon the Company by Parliament, shall cease and be null and void as respects so much thereof as then remains uncompleted.
This company is not in earnest. It asks for very extensive privileges, but practically assumes no responsibilities.
As you have just noted, it is stated at the outset of this clause that the company "may" be granted and as a matter of fact it is granted a delay of two years "to begin the construction of the railway lines" that clause 1 authorizes it to construct.
The reasons given by the hon. member in support of his bill permits us to foresee what certain persons intend to do should this bill be adopted. According to the statements made by the prime minister of Alberta and certain members of his cabinet, we note that the intention of all those who are interested in this project is simply, once the bill is passed, to sell their rights and hand over their charter to the National Railways. It is an open secret that on April 21, last, the prime minister of Alberta (Mr. Brownlee) came to Ottawa, and even went down to Montreal to consult the president of the National railways on the subject. Following this interview, he could not do otherwise than state that he hoped the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway Company would be purchased by the National railways.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
On the other hand, if we look up the history of the National Railway Company we can ascertain for ourselves that at various times private companies sold and conceded to this company, their rights, charter and stock, thus imposing on the ratepayere further expenses and taxes.
I shall go one step further, sir. I do not believe that the hon. member for Peace River is himself in earnest with regard to this bill, because in April last when this measure came up before the house, he could not supply the hon. Minister of Railways with information as to some figures. The hon. member should have had a knowledge of all the facts regarding this measure, moreover, this railway is on the south shore of the Peace River, while the majority of settlers are establshed on the northern side of the river. It is therefore seen that this railway will not be of any advantage or benefit, except to a few persons. This committee must not accept this bill nor grant the privileges sought to the detriment of the public's interest; the National railways have many improvements to make to their system, in every province of this Dominion, before ever thinking of purchasing a line which exists but in the minds of its promoters. Usually, when a company obtains a charter to build a railway, it is always cautious, through the medium of its engineers, to select the most adaptable roadway possible for the construction of its line; and when the time comes to sell its rights, if it succeeds, the company purchasing them is forced to pay a much higher price, many times more than what it is worth, because they cannot ignore those who obtained those rights. I believe that, in the present case, the intentions of the company do not differ from those of other companies which have acted likewise. In the past, railway branches where one could find but old ties and twisted rails, were sold a hundred times more than what they were worth. To-day we are loaded with an enormous debt; we have heavy interests to meet, and I am of the opinion that we should not add new taxes to those which already heavily burden the ratepayers.
Mr. Chairman, this question must not be discussed in a light manner; this bill should be returned to the committee on railways to be closely studied.
