I do not want to delay
the house, but I wish to refer to the case of the keeper of the Brandy Pot lighthouse. The present keeper is in class 7 and I would ask the department to put him in class 5, for the reasons I have already given. I have obtained some information from Mr. Hawken, the acting deputy minister, who tells me that it is hard to do anything more. If it is impossible to promote Mr. Dube, the keeper of this lighthouse, from class 7 to class 5 I will ask the committee to reduce the salary of the acting deputy minister to $1,200 a year, which is the salary being paid the lighthouse keeper at Brandy Pot.
The second point to which I wish to direct the attention of the committee is very simple. There is another lighthouse between Temis-couata county and the Tadoussac river, on Red Islet, which is a small island in the middle of the river. The lighthouse keeper there, and the lighthouse keeper at Notre Dame de Pile Verte, both need sailing vessels, because there are no bridges between these islands and the mainland and they have to carry barrels of gasoline or oil and other things for the lighthouse in addition to articles required for their personal use. I will ask the minister to give instructions that the lighthouse keepers at Red Islet and Notre Dame de Pile Verte be provided with sailing vessels of the ordinary size, such as they formerly had.
What salary does this lighthouse keeper receive now?
I spoke about two different things; I mentioned the lighthouse keeper at Brandy Pot and now I ask for sailing vessels for the other two lighthouse keepers.

I am not in a position to give a definite answer to my hon. friend now because I am not familiar with the conditions to which he has referred, but I can promise him that I will look into the matter and will do the best I can to meet his requests.



Sxipply-Marine and Fisheries

I have a matter I want to
bring up under this item; I refer to the holidays of the lighthouse keepers. It appears that a petition was presented to the government about two months ago by the Amalgamated Society of Civil Servants of Canada, which is the largest association of civil servants in Canada, drawing attention to the position of lighthouse keepers in relation to their annual leave. As the matter now stands, a lighthouse keeper taking an annual holiday has to provide and pay for a substitute during this leave of absence, and also has to assume responsibility during that period. I may explain that it is not so easy for a private person to obtain a substitute, and in addition it is very expensive for him to pay the steamer fare to his particular lighthouse. Moreover, he not only has to pay for the substitute but he also must be responsible for any action of that man, who may inadvertently do something to damage the machinery, for which the wretched lighthouse keeper, who is no more responsible than I am, must suffer the penalty, either by paying for the damage or by losing his position.
I will read from a letter which I have received:
For some considerable time lighthouse keepers have considered this an injustice, in view of the fact that other civil servants are not under this disadvantage, but are paid for their leave of absence.
I may state that these lighthouse keepers are civil servants in every sense of the word; they are under the act, and there is no opportunity of side-stepping by saying that they do not come under the act. They are under the act; thfey are appointed by the Civil Service Commission, so they are entitled to the same advantages enjoyed by the other civil servants. This letter goes on to say:
It has also been considered that, were the matter discussed impartially, the justice of the lighthouse keepers' plea for treatment similar to other civil servants could hardly be denied.
They evidently are not familiar with the customs and usages of the House of Commons at Ottawa. We have heard a great deal lately about freedom of speech; there is such a thing, Mr. Chairman, as the rights of the minority, which is sometimes quoted in the same connection. I have an idea that if these people numbered 6,000, as the civil servants do in Ottawa, instead of being scattered throughout the country, their demands would be acceded to, and the justice of their case would have been recognized long ere this. Surely

we are not going to say that the government is actuated by political expediency rather than by justice. These .people have no political pull whatever; they are scattered throughout the country and there are only a few in any one district. I do not suppose there are twenty lighthouses in the district I represent, and probably only about half the keepers would be able to vote because it is impossible for them to leave their lighthouses and travel the long distances necessary to get to the polls. So I do not expect any political or personal advantage from my plea to-night; it is made simply on the merits of the case.
I believe the civil servants at Ottawa have twenty-one days annual leave as holidays-it is provided for by the department-but in addition to that, whether it is a matter of custom or law, they are allowed two weeks' sick leave annually. If they have a casual cold or a headache produced by being out at a dance the night before, they are allowed their sick leave without a doctor's certificate, as long as it does not exceed two weeks in the year. When they have a real sickness, and a doctor's certificate is produced, they are again leniently dealt with. I have no objection to this at all, but I am only drawing a comparison between the life of a civil servant in Ottawa, with all the attendant social advantages, and at least five weeks' leave in the year, and the men out on a barren rock who get three weeks' leave if they supply a substitute and pay his wages and are responsible for anything he may do in that period.
I sometimes think it is a good thing to bring an argument home to ourselves. I wonder how many hon. members of this house would like to be stuck on an isolated light station month in and month out, year in and year out, hardly able to take even the necessary exercise, because there are no facilities for walking, no chance for any kind of amusement, no hobby, no one to associate with but one's wife. I have no desire to belittle the blessings of married life-I dare not do it if I would because though my wife does not read Hansard some busybody would be sure to draw her attention to it-I do not wish to deprecate the blessings of married life at all, but when a dieit is composed entirely of sweetness even it becomes unpalatable in time. I remember hearing a lecture many years ago by the Arctic explorer Nansen. He described how he and his partner had to spend a winter in a remote part of the Arctic region. These men were bound together by the ties of mutual friendship, and you would think they would have been glad to associate with each other, but he told how they would start out in the

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
morning without any conversation; -one would go east and the other west in order to get away from each other's society. They would return in the evening and there would be no conversation at all except that compelled by their joint interest. He said that he was able to laugh at it afterwards, and they remained friends, but the fact of there being such ill-will between them was so unjustified that it apparently made it much worse; they simply hated each other. This is the condition which might arise between a man and his wife when they are placed on a barren rock somewhere off the coast of British Columbia. They have nothing to look at except the wave-tossed sea. It rains there six months in the year, and it can rain more in two' days there than it does here in the whole year. If you think that is a nice prospect to look out at year after year, you are a better judge than I am.
I am emphasizing this case on behalf of the all-year-round permanent men, and not the men who are paid $15 a month to go out and light a light every night. I am speaking for the men who are employed twenty-four hours in the day every day in the year, not the men who attend these petty little lights where they can go out in an hour's time and do everything required. I suggest that these permanent men have a legal claim. I could read the whole adt if necessary to impress it on the committee, but the act provides that civil servants shall have three weeks holidays per year, and it does not say that they shall have to provide out of their own pockets for a substitute, transport him over a hundred miles, and be responsible for his errors.

I do not wish to delay the house, but I should like to say a few words on behalf of the lighthouse keepers, not only along the British Columbia coast, but along the Atlantic coast as well. I agree with everything the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said here to-night. I wonder how many people in Canada realize the lives that are lived year in and year out by these wonderful, heroic people who are guarding our seacoasts. There are twelve or thirteen lighthouses in the constituency I represent, and I visited five or six of them last year and found conditions prevailing which I am sure will appeal to the minister and to the government as deserving of consideration. These people have no holidays; if they need a holiday they must get a substitute and pay him from their slender salaries. These salaries range from $517.50 minimum to a maximum of $2,940 per year. I consider it an absolute
duty tlhat these people be given at least a fortnight's holiday, and they should not be obliged to pay the substitutes out of their small incomes. I am confident that the people of Canada one and all would be in accord with any move in that direction.
I visited a certain lighthouse where a man and his wife lived, and they told me a story so pathetic and so realistic that it would touch the chord of any heart that was responsive to any appeal to human kindness. Here is the story: Every month or so the feeling of isolation and loneliness played upon them to such an extent that one or the other would get into a deep fit of melancholy. For some three years neither of them could understand the other, and they lived a tragic life until one day it. dawned upon the husband that his wife was not at fault. They agreed upon a compromise whereby when either of them got into one of these melancholy moods, say if the wife refused to get breakfast in the morning and moped around the island rock, the husband would do the work instead. This depression would often last for a week, and then the wife would recover, but a fortnight later the husband might fall into one of these moods. They had tended this lighthouse for six years without any holidays. Surely we are not so hardhearted as to take the attitude that those who hold the frontier, those who endure this isolation, are not entitled to a little consideration. Surely they deserve at least a fortnight's holiday without being obliged to pay for a substitute out of their earnings. I am sure it would meet with the approbation of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and everybody else who listens to the story.

For Bird rocks, northeast Belle Isle and Pelee passage, the present salary is $2,820 out of which they have to pay three assistants. This is evidence enough to the committee that this class of servants needs looking into. To

I would not like it to go forth that anyone was asking, on a plea of this kind, for an expenditure of $200,000. There must be a very big mistake about that. The total expenditure asked for salaries and allowances for every kind of lightkeeper is $750,000. Many of them would be part time men not

I am thoroughly in accord with the remarks that have been made by my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi and my hon. friend from Skeena. I think this is one branch of the service that should receive every consideration from the department. I certainly
do not think that these men are overpaid; in fact, they 'are not paid enough. The fact that their salaries have increased since 1911 is no indication that they are being adequately paid to-day. I understand that in the service there are many lighthouses that are not in isolated positions at all, and where the lighthouse tender may live half a mile or a mile away from the light. The increase over last fiscal year is to provide for an extension of the service to meet the requirements of the air board by way of furnishing immediate data with regard to atmospheric conditions, air currents and so on, in particular districts and along particular routes.
How much was spent last year?

Item agreed to.
Steamboat inspection, $142,980.
This vote provides for an expenditure, but the government is practically reimbursed through the fees charged for this inspection and the money is paid into the consolidated revenue fund.
Do you inspect all passenger steamboats in Canada?

Will you give us the
income and expenditures for last year?
They have not been tabulated for last year, but I can give my hon friend an idea from the figures for 1926-27- the income was $135,450.39, and the expenditures amounted to $121,961.

Does this vote cover the
inspection of passenger steamships and lifesaving apparatus?
Yes.

How many inspectors are
there on this work?
About thirty-four in all.
How many classes of lifesaving apparatus are there?

I regret I have not the
regulations here.

If I read the reports correctly there is a No. 1 class, No. 2, No. 3, and so on. I am asking particularly with regard to the pleasure boats running on the Toronto-Kingston apd Kingston-Montreal lines. Does the department demand that these passenger boats shall have all No. .1 class life saving equipment, or do they still have considerable of what the department terms No. 2 and No. 3?
Not having the regulations before me, Mr. Chairman, I am not in position to satisfy my hon. friend regarding that. I will be quite ready to give him the information, probably to-morrow.

To my mind there is not
sufficient protection on these passenger boats -I am dealing particularly with the Ontario district-for the travelling public, especially during the tourist season when these boats are overcrowded. I suggest to the minister that this inspection should be reviewed and checked up to prevent the occurrence of a tragedy on our lakes in the near future.

What control has
the department over the number of passengers carried on boats?
According to the regulations, the inspector fixes the number of passengers that the boat can carry.

And a certificate to that effect is in the boat. But what

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
control has the department over the boat to see that this is carried out?

The customs collector at
the different ports is supposed to see that the regulations are observed.

And that is the
only official?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous-to provide for the salary of Hon. J. C. Patterson, commissioner to investigate titles of Great Britain to lands in the Arctic seas, $2,400.
I would like some information regarding this item.

The Hon. J. C. Patterson was appointed a commissioner to investigate titles of great Britain to lands in the Arctic seas by order in council P.C. 1160, at a salary of $200 per month, payable out of the moneys appropriated for unforeseen expenses. By order in council P.C. 1391 it was provided that Mr. Patterson's salary was to be paid out of moneys appropriated for the Canadian Arctic expedition organized in that year, and later designated as the patrol of northern waters of Canada. No provision being made in the main estimates for the fiscal year 1928-29 for the patrol of northern waters of Canada, some other provision for Mr. Patterson s salary is therefore necessary.
What is .tlhe explanation as to the need for the investigation of these titles?
He is working up some data and information to ascertain exactly the situation in regard to the lands which are mentioned in the order in council.
In regard to titles to lands of Great Britain?
Yes.
Why does Great Britain not look after her own titles?

These will be Canadian
lands.
The question naturally arises why Canada should investigate the titles of British lands. That is why we are asking the question.
Really they are Canadian.

It might be advisable to correct the item -and say: "titles of Ganad-a ". Now that we are on an equal status with
Great Britain I think we should investigate the titles of our lands and Great Britain might investigate the titles of hers.
Carried.
As amended.

Item agreed to.
Civil Government-Marine and Fisheries- salaries and contingencies, $614,615.

I must protest against the manner in whi-ch the Chairman (Mr Bouchard) is reading these items. We do not' know where we are and we cannot hear a word he says. I suggest that unless he speaks louder, some other hon. member should take the chair.
This is item 16, civil government. The details appear o-n page 87.

The increase of $4,500 is
due just to statutory increases?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Fisheries-salaries and disbursements of fishery officers and guardians, fisheries patrol and fisheries protection service, $950,000.
Mr. SHOR r: This is in connection with fisheries and as this is Friday, it is a good day to_ discuss them. I should like to say just a few words in connection with fisheries.
How many?

I will not talk too long. I have not a great deal of correspondence to read and I -hope hon. gentlemen will give me the same attention that they did the other rngh-t. If they wish to make any comments I shall be glad to have them and will answer them as best I can.
Make it short.

I will make it very short. Little or nothing has been done by the department of fisheries. I think the minister will agree with me that this is one department that has not received the attention it should receive. Had it received proper attention there would not have been the trouble or the discontent that occurred among the fishermen of the maritime provinces during the past year. When the Duncan report came d-own, one of the recommendations was that a deputy minister of fisheries should be appointed forthwith. When the discussion took place on that report, the Prime Minister, speaking on March 18, 1927, said, as reported in Hansard at page 1334:

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
The commission's recommendation with respect to the appointment of a deputy minister whose duties will be confined to what at present constitutes the fisheries section of the Department of Marine and Fisheries will be carried out.
A year and three months have elapsed since that statement was made to the house and no deputy minister has yet been appointed. Had that appointment been made shortly after the house prorogued last year, there would not have been the discontent that there was among the fishermen of the maritime provinces because they would have felt that something was being done for the industry. Nothing is being done for the industry by the department except to carry out the regulations that appear on the statute book or to put new ones into effect. Many of them which they should have carried out they did not carry out and those which they should not, they did carry out. If there is any department which has been neglected, it is the department of fisheries. I say this with all respect to the minister and the deputy. They are great friends of mine; I know they will take in all kindness everything I say, and I think down in their hearts they will agree with me. Both of them are very busy men. The marine department is a very large department and their time is practically taken up with it, the fisheries being left to other officials who have no power whatever. They must report to the deputy and the minister and, as I said before, they are too much engaged in the other duties of the department to bother about the fisheries.
Our fisheries constitute one of our greatest natural resources and if they were properly developed they would be capable of producing double the amount they do now. Last year the production of fish in this country amounted to about $50,000,000, and if we had a department of fisheries that amount could easily be doubled. The fisheries commission that has recently reported has gone further than the recommendations of the Duncan commission. They recommend that a separate department with a minister and a deputy be established. But I am not going to discuss that report tonight because I understand the Prime Minister has already stated to the house that as the government have not had an opportunity of going thoroughly, into the report, no legislation will be brought down this session in connection with the recommendations contained therein. Therefore the matter is not under discussion, unless the minister can give the committee an idea whether the government are going to change their minds or not. Will any action be
IMr. Short.]
taken in connection with the report this year? I presume not, because the minister does not answer. I presume they are not going to take any action, because one of the recommendations in the report was that no changes whatever should be made in the different seasons for taking lobsters in various sections of the province of Nova Scotia; that that regulation be made statutory so that it could be changed only by consent of parliament. But since the report was brought in a change has been made and an extension has already been given to one section of Nova Scotia. It is either ten or fifteen days, I do not know which. Evidently, therefore, the government do not intend to pay much attention to that report. Had we had a deputy minister appointed last year, we would never have had this trouble in connection with the fishermen in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. That commission has cost this country some $85,000. If that money had been spent in creating a separate department-and it would have carried that department for some time-it never would have been necessary to have a commission, because you would have had men in that fisheries department who knew something about the industry, and they would have brought down some remedies for the ills that exist in that part of the country. But the government decided that they would do nothing in that connection, and the result has been great deal of dissatisfaction and unrest among the fishermen of the maritime provinces, as the house is well aware
We feel also that we are not protected against foreign fish coming into this country Perhaps this house is not aware that we import from the United States nearly one million dollars' worth of fish a year. To be exact, last year we imported $911,000 worth of fish from the United States, practically every dollar's worth of which could have been produced in the maritime provinces. There was $540,000 worth of fresh fidh brought into Canada from the United States. Most of it came in last spring when prices were very low in the United States, and our duty of only one cent a pound is not sufficient protection to keep that fish from coming in, owing to the fact that the express and freight rates are very much lower from Boston and Portland to Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa than the rates from the maritime provinces, the distance being so much less.

Mr. Chairman, I rise
to a point of order. We are not discussing the tariff, I submit.

We have to bring in the tariff in order to show you what is wrong with our fisheries. I do not think the hon. member

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
has read the report of the commission. When we ship this same fish to tihe United States, we have to pay a duty of two cents a pound. There is no reason why there should be one dollar's worth of fresh fish brought into this country from the United States. The maritime provinces are suffering from lack of markets for their fish. We have been asking this government for the last two years to try to extend our markets for us. Hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of American fish, the same as we produce here, are brought into this country, and no steps have been taken by the government to relieve the situation. W7e also imported into this country from the United States 8108,500 of dried, smoked and pickled fish, every dollar's worth of which could have been produced in the maritime provinces, and would have been if we had had a duty as high as the American duty. We have not been able to export any of our cheap fresh fish to the United States since the Fordney tariff came into effect. If we had a deputy minister who was a practical man, who knew the conditions as they exist in the maritime provinces and elsewhere throughout this country, and the conditions as to markets, we might get some relief. For the last year and a half the Canadian Fisheries Association have been trying to get this government to help them in advertising fish so as to increase our markets in Canada, but last year the government never contributed one dollar towards that advertising campaign. The year before they did contribute $10,000. and the industry had to put up a like amount; but. ten or twenty thousand dollars is not enough to carry on a propaganda of advertising in this country if we are going to increase the sale of our fish, which is one of our great natural products, giving employment to thousands of our Canadian citizens.

How many carloads of
fish were shipped from Athabaska to Detroit?

I could not tell you; that
is out of my district. Perhaps my hon. friend from .Skeena could answer that.
The hon. member for Rosetown ought to know.

It would be in the public
interest to appropriate in these estimates a sufficient amount to carry on an advertising propaganda in this country to increase the sale of fish. Had we had a market for our fish there never would have been any trouble with the fishermen. Our trouble has been lack of markets, and the consequence was the fishermen could not make a living. They felt that they had to make some appeal to the public, which they did, and the government
finally took notice of it and appointed this commission, which has dealt very thoroughly with the situation.
I see an item of $130,000 to assist in the conservation and development of the deep sea fisheries and the demand for fish. Why cannot a sum be taken from that item for advertising purposes, which would be of the greatest benefit to the country? This same item of $130,000 was in the estimates last year, and only $5,920 out of that $130,000 was expended. The department does not even seem to know how to expend the very small appropriation which they do get for the fisheries.
I say, therefore, that they should call in a practical man, a man who knows that business -because they have got the men. They should put in authority a man who knows production, and who knows how fish are sold. Last year they sent two men, Mr. Cowie, of the department, and a Mr. Earle, across to England to look into the question of markets for our fish, but I have not heard a word of what they did. It cost this country several thousands of dollars to send them over there. There is a market for our fish in England, but it is up to the department to develop that market, just as other departments of the government, the Department of Agriculture, for instance, develops markets for the products of the farm. But the department of fisheries has done nothing whatever in that regard. I am told that there is a wonderful prospect for a market for our fresh fish in England. But no single firm can develop that business, and it is therefore up to the government to find a market for our fish, just as it does for other natural products. That is what the Department of Fisheries is for, but absolutely nothing has been done'.
I do not want to be complaining. Mr. Chairman, at all. I just want to bring this matter to the attention of the committee for its consideration. I am not blaming the present minister a bit more than his predecessors. We have never had a practical man in charge of the fisheries department. What would the Department of Agriculture think if a professional man was made Minister of Agriculture? They have never done that, and why should we not have a man who knows the fish game in charge of the Fisheries department that you are going to establish? You want a man who knows the industry, and you have such a man on your side of the house, a man who is capable in every way, a man who has been in the fish business all his life and knows it from start to finish. I want to give a word of caution: when this separate department is created do not put in a clerical man who

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
knows nothing whatever about the business; put in a man who knows the industry, and then you will get some results. I bring this to the attention of the minister in the hope that something will foe done so that we will not next year have the same trouble down in our province that we had last.

Mr. Chairman, the government has decided to appeal to the Privy Council. I may reassure my hon. friend on another point. So long as there is an appeal to a higher tribunal the judgment of the lower court is of no effect. Consequently the situation remains as it was, the judgment of the supreme court can have no effect until it is affirmed by the Privy Council, and in the meantime we shall carry on in the usual way. So my hon. friend need not be afraid of the alarming developments to which he has referred.

I am very glad to hear the
minister express his opinion in this matter, both as a minister and a lawyer. While I would have preferred to see an amendment made to the Fisheries Act-and I think this is the course that ultimately will have to be taken-yet at this late stage of the session the decision announced foy the minister will perhaps be as effective as we could wish.
As to the remarks of my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short), of course he was entirely out of order; he was talking on an item that had nothing to do with the subject. It should have been brought up on the civil government estimates. However the hon. member has been allowed to deviate from the straight and narrow path and I may be allowed to do the same for a few minutes. I endorse what he has said as regards the appointment of a deputy minister. We were promised that, if not the year before last, certainly last year. The legislation has been passed and I see no reason why it should not be carried out.
It will be.

It would make for efficiency in the service. The Duncan report also recommended it and we in British Columbia are anxious to have the same thing. I would

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
go further, again following the Duncan report, and say that we in British Columbia are in sympathy with the idea of having a commissioner for the east and one ailso for the west-men who would live, respectively, in the maritime provinces and in British Columbia and who would necessarily be familiar with the local conditions of the industry. As my hon. friend has indicated, they would be able to formulate policies ahead, so to speak, of their urgent necessity and not wait until the industry was almost in the ditch. They would foresee trouble and devote themselves to the providing of remedies. Speaking for British Columbia and particularly for the district I represent, I hope that before long we shall see the Department of Fisheries established under the deputy minister.

I want to refer to
another matter. Yesterday we listened to the hon. member for Comox-Albemi speaking in regard to the conditions of men employed in the life saving stations in British Columbia. He referred to their pay and also to the fact that they are not under the Civil Service Commission, being thereby deprived of certain privileges which otherwise they would enjoy. There is another Class that comes directly under this item; I refer to the patrol boat employees on the Pacific coast. I have from time to time made representations to the department, and representations have also been made by the Amalgamated Civil Servants' Association of New Westminster in the same connection. These men are very much underpaid, it seems to me, and more than that they have been deprived of certain perquisites which they formerly received. They formerly received food when they were out on their work; they got provisions; and they have been deprived of these. They were not granted any increase of pay when other civil servants received an increase; it was stated that they were not permanent employees. All I can say in that connection is that a great many of these men have been in the employ of the department for upwards of five, ten and fifteen years. To say that they are only temporary employees seems to me rather ridiculous. They are not given any holidays at all; nor are they entitled to any superannuation. They work from seventy to eighty hours a week for five months of the year and during the remaining months the}' work a minimum of forty-four hours per week. I do not think the government is treating the civil servants of this country at all fairly in a great many ways, and this particular class have been very
badly treated. There is no reason whatever in the stand taken by the department, that these men are not entitled to further consideration. Their salaries are most inadequate and I would impress upon the minister the necessity for reveiwing the condition of these men. I would also ask that he do something to give them fair treatment. It was my privilege to bring the matter to the attention of the minister personally, but T am afraid he has not gone into it very carefully, because he cannot defend the stand which the department has taken.
Will the minister explain the increase?

The flat increase of $120 given last year was paid out of the special appropriation; this year it is included here. It amounts to $9,500. This year the annual increases amount to $1,860. Two new boats for the Atlantic coast are required; one for investigational work, $12,000 and one to replace hired boats for the Grand Manan district for which we are paying $600 per year. The new boat will cost about $2,000 and will pay for itself in less than four years. This amounts to $14,000. There are also new boats for the Pacific, one to replace the Swan, built in 1908 and which is worn out; the other takes the place of a boat which was burned last fall. At $6,000 each these amount to $12,000. There is a new engine for another vessel; this amounts to $3,000. This makes up the $40,000 increase.
But I understand there is an increase of $90,000.

We had a supplementary
voted at the opening of this session for last year amounting to $50,000.

Is there any of this
money spent in the prairie provinces?
Yes.
How much?
The expenditure in Manitoba last year was $16,618.96; Saskatchewan, $18,588.66; Alberta, $21,391.73. This is for fishery officers.
What are the duties of these officers?
They are administering the fishery laws and seeing that the regulations are observed.

We often hear complaints about the number of inspectors in the Department of Agriculture, and I was just wonder-

,	Supply-Marine and Fisheries
ing, for the purpose of comparison, how many inspectors are included under this vote.
In the three prairie provinces there are three district inspectors, fifteen overseers and twenty-four guardians.
What is the duty of an overseer? Does he oversee the inspector?
No, he sees that the regulations in his district are observed. He has charge of a particular district.
Would the minister just go a little further and tell us what he does in that district? What is the difference between an inspector and an overseer?

The inspector is the more important man. There is one inspector for each province, but he cannot see to all the details and supervise all the districts under his control. The men working under him are the overseers, who are given certain districts to look after, and these overseers have under them the guardians, who are supposed to see that the regulations are observed.

Are these guardians full-time men?
Mr. CARDIN. No, they are only seasonal men.
Mr. Chairman, I call your attention to the fact that it is eleven o'clock.
They are paid only the rate prevailing in that locality.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
